results.question: how long do i keep tax records
results.answer:
You should keep your tax‑related paperwork for the amount of time the IRS requires you to be able to use it to support or amend a return, and you may keep records longer if another purpose (e.g., a creditor or insurance company) requires them. The guidance in the IRS documents is:

* **General tax records** – Keep any records that support an item of income or deduction on a tax return until the *period of limitations* for that return expires. The period of limitations is the time during which you can amend a return or the IRS can reassess tax. For most income‑tax returns this is the number of years shown in the IRS table that applies to that return’s filing year (generally 3 years from the due date, but it can be longer if you failed to report income, filed a fraudulent return, etc.) **[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)**

* **Copies of filed returns** – Keep a copy of each tax return you file, because they are helpful when preparing future returns and for amended returns. **[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)**

* **Employment tax records** – If you have employees, keep all employment‑tax records for at least **four (4) years** after the date the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later. **[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)**

* **Asset‑related records** – Keep records relating to a property (depreciation, basis, sale, etc.) until the period of limitations expires for the year in which you dispose of the property in a taxable disposition. If you received property in a non‑taxable exchange, keep records for both the old and new property until the limitation period for the disposition of the new property ends. **[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)**

* **Non‑tax purposes** – If the IRS no longer needs the records for tax purposes, do not discard them until you confirm that no other party (e.g., an insurer, creditor, or state tax agency) requires a longer retention period. **[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)**

* **Electronic records** – The same retention periods that apply to paper books and records apply to any electronic storage system that is used to keep your books and records. **[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)**

In short, retain all supporting documents for each income or deduction until the period of limitations runs out, retain copies of the returns you file, hold employment‑tax records for at least four years, keep asset records until their limitation period ends, and only discard any records after you’ve confirmed no other agency or entity needs them longer.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)
2. [irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf (Page 12)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)

results.question: why do i need to keep business records
results.answer:
You need to keep business records for several concrete reasons that are spelled out in the IRS guidance:

1. **They let you run and monitor the business.**  “Good records can increase the likelihood of business success” and help you see which items are selling, whether costs are rising, and what changes you might need to make [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11).  They are also the data you use to prepare accurate income‑and‑loss statements and balance sheets for banks, creditors, and yourself [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11).

2. **They support your tax filings.**  Supporting documents (sales slips, invoices, bank deposit slips, etc.) are required to back up every entry in your books and on your tax return.  The IRS can request them during an examination, and “a complete set of records will speed up the examination” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12).

3. **They satisfy legal and regulatory requirements.**  For example, employment‑tax records must be kept for at least 4 years after the tax becomes due, and property‑depreciation records must be kept until the limitations period on the year you dispose of the asset ends [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16).  Keeping records also allows you to prove that receipts are business income rather than personal, which is required for correct tax reporting [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12).

4. **They protect you from penalties.**  If your electronic storage system (or paper books) doesn’t meet IRS rules, you can be subject to penalties.  Maintaining accurate, complete, and legible records keeps you in compliance and avoids these penalties [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12).

5. **They enable you to claim deductions and credits.**  The IRS needs the underlying evidence (e.g., car‑expense receipts, home‑office calculations, depreciation schedules) to approve the deductions and credits you claim [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11).

6. **They provide evidence for your business plans, loan applications, and investment needs.**  Lenders and investors ask for the last three years of personal and business tax returns, financial statements, and other records to evaluate your business [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16).

In short, without records you cannot prove income, claim deductions, respond to IRS requests, or manage your business effectively—all of which can result in penalties, missed tax savings, or operational failure.

results.question: what accounting method should i use
results.answer:
The IRS lets you choose one of several approval‑under‑rule accounting methods when you file your first business tax return (Form 1040 with Schedule C).  The choice depends on what kind of business you run, whether you keep inventory, and how large the business is.

| Situation | Recommended method (per the IRS guidance) | Why |
|-----------|-------------------------------------------|-----|
| **You’re a sole proprietor or single‑member LLC with **no inventory** and you want the simplest books** | **Cash method** | “Most individuals and many sole proprietors with no inventory use the cash method because they find it easier to keep cash method records.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |
| **You keep inventory or sell merchandise in the ordinary course of business** | **Accrual method** (unless you qualify for a small‑business exception – see §7) | “If an inventory is necessary … you must generally use an accrual method of accounting for sales and purchases.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |
| **You have inventory but your inventory is treated as “non‑incidental material or supplies” and you meet the small‑business limits** | **Cash method for inventory items** (or overall cash method) | “Certain small business taxpayers can use the cash method … and can also account for inventoriable items as materials and supplies that are not incidental.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16) |
| **You need to combine cash and accrual rules for different items** | **Combination method** (possible if the combination clearly shows income and is used consistently) | “You can generally use any combination of cash, accrual, and special methods … as long as the combination clearly shows your income.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |
| **You intend to change your method in the future** | File Form 3115 (Application for Change in Accounting Method) and obtain IRS approval. | “After that, if you want to change your accounting method, you must generally get IRS approval.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14) |

**Key Points to Remember**

1. **Choose at first return** – The method you pick when you file your first tax return with Schedule C becomes your business accounting method.  
2. **Consistency** – Use the same method to figure profit and to keep your books.  
3. **Inventory rule** – If you sell products that are held for sale, you usually must use the accrual method for those sales and purchases, unless you qualify for the small‑business inventory exception.  
4. **Changing methods** – Changing later requires Form 3115 and may need a user fee if you’re not in an "automatic" category.  
5. **Business vs personal** – You can use different methods for business and personal items, and for multiple independent businesses you may use separate methods if each clearly shows its own income.  

So, if your business is simple, has no inventory, and you want the easiest bookkeeping, choose the **cash method**. If you keep inventory, or sell goods that must be inventoried, choose the **accrual method** (or the small‑business cash + inventory option if it applies). If you have more complex needs, a **combination method** may be appropriate. Always keep consistent records and, if you change, file Form 3115 to get IRS approval.



**Sources:**
1. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 14)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)
2. [irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf (Page 16)](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)

results.question: how do i check my workplace for hazards
results.answer:
To check your workplace for hazards, follow the step‑by‑step approach that the handbook recommends.  

### 1. Conduct a routine workplace self‑inspection  
* Have knowledgeable employees inspect the work area themselves.  
* Use the handbook’s self‑inspection checklists as a starting point.  
* The goal is to “identify hazards, control identified hazards, and monitor and evaluate hazard controls to verify that they continue to be effective.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

### 2. Gather supporting information  
Collect data from:  
* Injury and illness records (e.g., OSHA Form 300).  
* Worker training records.  
* Process and equipment logs (maintenance, failure reports).  
* Any other records that indicate work‑related incidents.  
Combine these records with the completed checklists to see where hazards or control gaps exist. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=8)

### 3. Identify and assess hazards  
Apply the handbook’s seven‑core‑element framework:  
1. Management leadership  
2. Worker participation  
3. Hazard identification and assessment  
4. Hazard prevention and control  
5. Education and training  
6. Program evaluation and improvement  
7. Communication and coordination  

This structure keeps the safety focus systematic and repeatable. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)

### 4. Check specific risk areas  
Use the targeted checklists for particular hazards such as:  
* Chemical hazards (labeling, SDS, hazardous‑chemical inventory).  
* Housekeeping and housekeeping flow (clutter, wet surfaces, waste storage).  
* Walking‑working surfaces and access routes.  
* Confined spaces, lock‑out/tag‑out practices, PPE, and first‑aid/ emergency prep.  

Each checklist’s **“Comments”** section signals whether you have met the requirement or need improvement. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=38)[[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=11)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=79)

### 5. Document findings and corrective actions  
Record each hazard found, the control you plan or have implemented, and the timeline for completion. Keep this data in your safety and health program records so you can monitor whether the controls remain effective. [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=9)

### 6. Use additional resources if needed  
If your self‑inspection shows complex hazards or you want external help, contact:  

* **OSHA On‑Site Consultation Program** – free, confidential visits by trained consultants to help identify hazards and create improvement plans. [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90)  
* **Compliance Assistance Specialists** – available to discuss standards and controls. [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=91)  

### 7. Repeat the process regularly  
Hazards change as tasks, equipment, or personnel change. Re‑inspect at least annually—or more often if your situation warrants—to keep the workplace safe. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7)

---

**Summary**:  
1. Use the handbook’s self‑inspection checklists.  
2. Collect injury, training, and equipment records.  
3. Identify and assess hazards using the seven‑element safety program framework.  
4. Review specific hazard categories with their checklists.  
5. Document findings and plan/implement controls.  
6. Seek OSHA On‑Site consultation if needed.  
7. Repeat the inspection periodically.  

These steps give you a structured, documented, and OSHA‑approved way to spot and control workplace hazards.

results.question: cash or accrual accounting whats the difference
results.answer:
Cash vs. accrual accounting are two basic ways a business can match its income and expenses to a tax year.  

**Cash method**  
* Income is reported in the year it is actually received (or when it is constructively received).  
* Expenses are deducted in the year they are paid (or when the payment is made).  
* The example in Segment 1 shows how a business can deduct office‑supplies in 2025 even though the bill is paid in 2026, because the cash method counts the expense when the cash leaves the company.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)  
* Cash accounting is normally used by sole‑proprietors, partners, and small businesses that have no inventory, because it is easier to keep track of money that actually changes hands.  
* If a business must keep inventory, the IRS generally requires it to use the accrual method for the sales and purchases that relate to that inventory, even if it otherwise uses cash.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)  

**Accrual method**  
* Income is reported in the year it is earned—when the “all‑events” test is met (the right to receive is fixed and the amount can be reasonably determined).  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  
* Expenses are deducted in the year they are incurred—when economic performance has occurred (the cost has been used or the service delivered).  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  
* The IRS encourages the accrual method because it matches revenue and related expenses in the same period, giving a clearer picture of profit, especially for businesses that keep inventory.  
* Example from Segment 1: an office‑supplies purchase bought in December 2025 but paid in January 2026 can still be deducted in 2025 under accrual because the liability is fully established in 2025.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=16)  
* For service contracts, the accrual method requires you to accrue the basic rate of income even if the contract is paid later (the “change in payment schedule” rule).  [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15)  

**Key differences**  
| Feature | Cash method | Accrual method |
|---------|-------------|----------------|
| **When income is recognized** | When cash is received (or constructively received) | When earned (all‑events test) |
| **When expenses are deducted** | When cash is paid | When incurred (economic performance) |
| **Inventory requirement** | Can be used if no inventory; if inventory exists, usually must switch to accrual for those items | Required for businesses that sell or produce inventory |
| **Simplicity** | Easier to maintain; suitable for small, cash‑centric businesses | More complex; better for businesses that want a true financial picture or have inventory |
| **Financial matching** | Periodic income may not match the expenses that produced it | Income and related expenses are matched in the same period |

In short, **cash accounting** follows the flow of money, while **accrual accounting** follows the decision to earn and the consumption of resources, giving a more accurate picture of profitability when a business has inventory or long‑term contracts.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)



**Sources:**

results.question: can i deduct business travel
results.answer:
Yes – you can deduct the ordinary and necessary costs of traveling away from home for business.  
The IRS allows you to claim:

* **Transportation** – airfare, train, bus, or car mileage (actual expenses or the standard mileage rate), taxi, limousine, commuter bus fares, tolls, parking fees, and the cost of sending baggage or display items between your regular place of business and a temporary workplace.  
* **Meals and lodging** – if the trip is overnight or long enough that you must sleep or rest to perform your duties. You may use actual expenses or the standard meal allowance, and normally only 50 % of meal costs are deductible.  
* **Other travel‑related items** – dry‑cleaning, laundry, telephone communications, and tips related to travel.  

You may not deduct ordinary commuting costs between your home and your main or regular workplace, but you can deduct any travel between different business locations or a temporary workplace and your regular office.  

If you use a car for business travel, you can choose between the standard mileage rate (for 2025 it is $0.70 per mile) or actual costs, but you must apportion business versus personal use.  

These rules are set out in Pub. 463 and the instructions for Schedule C (Form 1040) and are summarized in segments 1, 2, and 3 of the provided text.  

[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=41)[[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=40)[[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=35)

results.question: what goes in an executive summary
results.answer:
The executive summary is a short, focused overview that tops a business plan. According to the guide, it should be brief—usually one or two paragraphs—and cover the following points: describe your business idea, state how much money you need and what it will be used for, indicate how much capital you have already invested (or will invest) in the business, and provide a brief timeline of your major goals or milestones. Because some of these details may only be known after the rest of the plan is finished, the executive summary is typically written last.

results.question: how do i describe my target market
results.answer:
To describe your target market you should:

1. **Define the niche** – say who your “best” customers are.  
   *Example:* “Our best customers are young families (age 35–45) who live within a 10‑mile radius of the store, have a household income of $60‑$90 k, and buy organic, gluten‑free produce.”  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

2. **List characteristics** – describe demographics (age, gender, income, education), psychographics (lifestyle, values), geographic location, and behavior (purchase frequency, buying motives).  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

3. **Segment the market** – use categories such as industry or company size for business markets, or age, gender, income, lifestyle for consumer markets.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

4. **Estimate size and growth** – use population figures, industry stats, or sales tax data to estimate how big the segment is and how fast it’s growing.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

5. **Project your share** – explain what portion of that total market you expect to capture.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=14)

results.question: do i have to make my shop wheelchair accessible
results.answer:
Yes.  
The ADA requires that any private business that serves the public (a **public accommodation**) make its premises *Accessible*—unless the barrier is not “readily achievable.”  Existing businesses built before 1993 must still remove obvious, easily fixable barriers; otherwise they must provide an alternate service such as home‑delivery or an accessible entrance elsewhere.  [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)

For a shop, the key accessibility requirements include:

| Requirement | What the ADA calls for | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **Accessible entrance** | A ramp, automatic door, or other means that eliminates steps.  If a ramp is added, its slope must be no steeper than 1:12 and handrails are required when the rise is >6 in.  A wide landing (≥ 18 in) should be provided. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10) |
| **Accessible route** | A continuous, firm, slip‑resistant path with no steps or steep slopes, leading from the sidewalk to the interior sale or service areas. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10) |
| **Accessible counter** | For a sales/switch counter the accessible portion must be ≤ 36 in high and ≥ 36 in long, with a clear floor space of at least 30 in × 48 in in front. | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=15) |
| **Accessible parking** | At least one accessible parking space on level ground, with a 5‑ft wide access aisle and the international symbol of accessibility sign.  An accessible route must connect that space to the shop entrance. | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=8) |
| **Door hardware & turnstiles** | All door handles must be operable without a tight grasp; a round knob, lever, or loop is acceptable.  Narrow turnstiles must be replaced or bypassed by an accessible gate. | [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12) |
| **Barrier removal priority** | Remove the most obvious, physically simple barriers first (steps, narrow aisles, high counters).  If a barrier is not readily achievable, alternative services such as home‑delivery may be required. | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=7) |

If your shop already has a single entrance that cannot be made accessible, the ADA still requires either converting that entrance or adding a second accessible entrance, plus a sign directing customers to the accessible doorway.  A secured, locked accessible entrance must be unlocked for business hours; if that is not possible a staff‑available call box or buzzer is required.  [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)  

In short, under the ADA you *do* have to make your shop wheelchair accessible—or, if certain changes are not “readily achievable,” you must provide alternate ways for people with disabilities to obtain your goods or services.

results.question: am i exempt from injury recordkeeping
results.answer:
You are only partially exempt from OSHA’s injury‑and‑illness record‑keeping rules if one of the following conditions applies:

* **Your business had 10 or fewer employees during the entire previous calendar year.**  
  This is the 29 CFR 1904.1 exemption for small employers. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

* **Your business operates in certain low‑hazard industries listed in Subpart B, Appendix A of 29 CFR 1904.**  
  These industries are identified by the Bureau of Labor Statistics and include many offices, retail stores, salons, and light manufacturing, among others. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

Even if you qualify for either exemption, you must still:

* Report work‑related **fatalities**, **in‑patient hospitalizations**, **amputations**, and **loss of an eye** to OSHA without delay—fatalities within 8 hours, hospitalizations, amputations, and eye loss within 24 hours. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

If your business **does not meet** those exemption criteria, you must keep the usual OSHA injury records (Forms 300, 301, and 300A) and may need to submit the annual summary electronically if you have 250 + workers or, in certain high‑hazard industries, 20–249 workers. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)

So, determine whether you had 10 or fewer workers in the last calendar year or if your industry is on the low‑hazard list; that will tell you if you’re exempt from OSHA’s injury‑recordkeeping requirements.

results.question: what records do i keep for tax and for injuries and for how long
results.answer:
**Tax records**

* Keep copies of every tax return you file and all documents that support the income, deductions, or credits reported on that return.  
  *For example, retain receipts, invoices, bank statements, payroll records, and supporting documents that explain each entry in your books.* [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

* The length of time you must keep each type of tax record varies with the underlying tax.  
  * **Employment‑tax records** (wage‑withholding, Social‑Security, Medicare, FUTA, etc.) must be kept for **at least 4 years** after the tax becomes due or is paid, whichever is later. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
  * **Asset‑related records** (purchase, improvement, depreciation, sale, etc.) should be kept **until the period of limitation expires for the year you dispose of the asset**—usually 3–6 years after the sale or exchange. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  
  * In general, *tax‑related records that support income, deductions, or credits should be kept for the period of limitation applicable to the tax year on which the return was filed* (usually 3 years for most income‑tax returns, 6 years if a claim is based on more than 25 % of the return, and longer if you file a fraudulent return). [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

* If your records are stored electronically, the electronic system must preserve the data in a legible, complete, and retrievable format for the same period and may be destroyed only after it has been proven to produce the original records. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  

**Injury/Illness **records (OSHA)**

* **OSHA Form 300** (log of work‑related injuries and illnesses) and the supplemental **Form 301** (injury/illness incident report) must be kept in paper or electronic form for **at least 5 years** from the date they were entered or the year covered. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  
* The **annual summary, OSHA Form 300A**, must also be kept for **at least 5 years**. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  
* **Worker medical and exposure records** are retained for the time period required for each specific type of record, which varies by the nature of the exposure or condition. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15)  
* Employers with 10 or fewer workers or in low‑hazard industries may be partially exempt, but the OSHA requirements above apply to all other businesses. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=14)  

**Bottom line**

* For tax purposes, keep records long enough to cover the applicable period of limitation—most commonly 3‑6 years, with employment‑tax records kept for at least 4 years and asset‑related records until the disposal‑date limitation ends. Save copies of all filed returns.  

* For workplace injuries, keep OSHA logs, incident reports, and annual summaries for **5 years**, plus any worker medical or exposure records for the specific retention period dictated by their type.  

These retention periods are drawn directly from the IRS “Recordkeeping” guidance (Segment 1 and 2) and OSHA “Recordkeeping and Reporting” requirements (Segments 10 and 15).

results.question: how do i start a business and keep my taxes organized
results.answer:
**Starting a business and keeping your taxes organized**

1. **Choose a business structure**  
   • Pick the type of business you want—sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation, S‑corporation, or LLC.  
   • The choice determines the form you file for income tax, how you pay self‑employment tax, and which payroll or employment‑tax forms you must use.  
   “The form of business you operate determines which income‑tax return form you have to file.” [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=3)  

2. **Get an Employer Identification Number (EIN) and other taxpayer IDs**  
   • Most businesses need an EIN; individuals without employees can use their SSN or, if they prefer, an EIN.  
   • If you have foreign partners or employees, you may need a payee’s identification number or an ITIN.  
   “You must also have an EIN to use as a TIN if you do either of the following.” [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=6)  

3. **Decide on a tax year**  
   • Adopt a calendar tax year (Jan‑Dec) or a fiscal year (12 consecutive months ending on a month other than December).  
   • The chosen year is set when you file your first return; changing it later requires Form 1128 and IRS approval.  
   “You must adopt the calendar‑tax year if any of the follow‑ing apply.” [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)  
   “If you want to change your accounting method, you must generally get IRS approval.” [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  

4. **Pick an accounting method**  
   • **Cash method** – record income when received and expenses when paid.  
   • **Accrual method** – record income when earned and expenses when incurred.  
   • An inventory‑holding business usually must use accrual.  
   “Under the cash method, you report income in the tax year you receive it.” [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  

5. **Open a separate business bank account & use a business checkbook**  
   • Keep business funds separate from personal accounts.  
   • Record each transaction (deposits, withdrawals, expenses) in a business checkbook or an electronic system that can produce legible copies for the IRS.  
   “You should keep your business account separate from your personal checking account.” [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)  

6. **Maintain accurate, organized records**  
   • Keep a summary of income and expenses (journals/ledgers), supporting documents (receipts, invoices, deposit slips), and business‑specific records for each separate business.  
   • Electronic records are acceptable if they can be reproduced in legible form.  
   “The original hard copy books and records may be destroyed provided that the electronic storage system has been tested …” [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  
   “You must keep your records as long as they may be needed … Generally, 3‑7 years.” [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=16)  

7. **Deductible business expenses**  
   • Ordinary and necessary costs (supplies, rent, advertising, travel, a portion of utilities, car expenses, etc.) can be deducted on Schedule C, Schedule E, or other appropriate schedules.  
   “You can deduct business expenses on your business or personal income tax return … The expense must be both ordinary and necessary.” [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=32)  

8. **Pay taxes on time**  
   • **Self‑employment tax** – pay by estimated payments (Form 1040‑ES) if you expect $1,000+ in tax.  
   • **Employment taxes** – file Form 941 quarterly (or Form 944 annually) and remit withheld payroll taxes.  
   • **Income‑tax return** – File Form 1040‑S, Schedule C, etc., by the 15th day of the 4th month after year‑end, unless an extension is filed.  
   • **Estimated tax payment deadlines** – 15 th day of the 4th, 6th, 9th months and the 1st month after year‑end.  
   “If you expect to owe tax of $1,000 or more, you generally have to make estimated tax payments…” [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=6)  
   “Due by 15th day of the 4th month after the end of the tax year.” [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11)  

9. **File information returns (when needed)**  
   • Issue Form 1099‑MISC for rent, royalties, prizes, etc.; Form 1099‑NEC for non‑employee compensation ≥$600.  
   • Provide copies to recipients by Jan 31 and to the IRS by Feb 28 (or Mar 31 if electronic).  
   “Form 1099‑NEC, Nonemployee Compensation… by January 31.” [[11]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=12)  

10. **Stay organized for audits and future returns**  
    • Keep copies of filed returns and supporting documents.  
    • Reconcile your bank statement to the business checkbook each month.  
    “By reconciling your checking account each month…” [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)  

**Bottom line**  
Start by deciding your legal form, obtain an EIN, set your tax year and accounting method, open a dedicated bank account, keep meticulous records and receipts, file the correct return and payroll or estimated‑tax forms on time, and file any required information returns. Following these steps keeps your business compliant and your taxes organized.

results.question: what do i need to do to keep employees safe and my premises accessible
results.answer:
To keep your workers safe **and** make your premises accessible you need a two‑part plan:  
1.  A workplace‑safety program that protects employees from accidents and health hazards, and  
2.  An ADA‑compliant accessibility strategy that removes physical barriers and supports customers and employees with disabilities.  
Below are the concrete steps you should take, with each fact drawn directly from the provided segments.

---

## 1.  Create and maintain a safety and health program  

| Action | What it involves | Source |
|--------|------------------|--------|
| **Leadership commitment** – set clear goals, assign responsibility, and allocate resources | Management leads the program, sets hazards‑inspection schedules, and reviews results | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7) |
| **Worker participation** – involve employees in safety committees or meetings | Staff help identify hazards and review corrective actions | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7) |
| **Hazard identification & assessment** – perform regular workplace inspections | Identify slip‑trips, falling objects, machinery hazards, etc. | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=6) |
| **Preventive controls** – install guardrails, machine‑shutdown switches, proper lighting | Keep walkways clear and slip‑resistant | [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=94) |
| **Education & training** – train workers on safe practices, use of PPE, emergency response | Provide classroom or on‑the‑job instruction | [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=7) |
| **Program evaluation** – review incident logs, inspection reports, and training records | Adjust the program based on findings | [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=6) |
| **Emergency action plan** – define evacuation routes, call procedures, and special‑needs assistance | Incorporate disability considerations | [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=26)[[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=27) |
| **Recordkeeping** – maintain OSHA 300/301 logs for five years, report fatalities within 8 h | Keep logs at the worksite for at least five years | [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=15) |
| **Consultation** – use OSHA On‑Site Consultation for free, confidential advice | Consult state‑approved programs if available | [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/319-osha_small_business_handbook.pdf#page=90) |

These steps satisfy OSHA’s “General Duty Clause” and reduce injury costs, improve morale, and keep your business compliant.  

---

## 2.  Make the premises accessible to people with disabilities  

| Barrier | What to do | Source |
|---------|-----------|--------|
| **Entrance / door** | • Ensure at least one entrance is **36 in. wide** or has a ramp with a 1:12 slope and handrails when the rise > 6 in. | [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=10)[[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/316-ada_guide_small_business.pdf#page=11) |

results.question: how do i write a business plan and set up accounting
results.answer:
**How to write a business plan**

1. **Cover page** – put the company name, address, phone number, owners, and the date of the plan. Add a logo if you have one. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  
2. **Table of contents** – optional, but useful for long plans. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  
3. **Executive summary** – one‑two paragraphs summarizing the idea, the amount of money needed, how you’ll use it, and your short‑term schedule of goals. Write this section last because it pulls together information you’ve gathered later. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  
4. **Business description** – explain your product or service, the market, and how you will maintain a competitive advantage. Discuss any industry regulations, licenses, or certifications you will need. [[2]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=12)  
5. **Management plan** – outline the ownership structure (sole‑proprietorship, partnership, LLC, etc.). List the day‑to‑day manager, long‑term planner, and key personnel, and provide brief resumes or credentials. Include an exhibit sheet of legal documents if needed. [[3]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=13)  
6. **Market analysis** – describe total addressable market, target customers, competition, and how you plan to reach and sell to your customers. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)  
7. **Financial (money) section** – include:
   * **Sources and uses of funds** statement  
   * **Three‑year income projection** (monthly for each year)  
   * **Cash‑flow projection** (monthly for each year)  
   * **Balance sheet** (as of a fixed date, e.g., month‑end)  
   * **Break‑even analysis** (show dollar amount or units needed to cover operating costs)  
   These documents let lenders see if the business can fund itself and grow. [[4]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=16)  
8. **Exhibits** – attach resumes, purchase agreements, bids, contracts, floor plans, a copy of the sources‑and‑uses sheet, and any other supporting documentation. [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=4)

**How to set up accounting**

1. **Open a business‑checking account** that is separate from any personal account. Use it for every income and expense deposit/withdrawal. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)  
2. **Choose an accounting method** when you file your first tax return:
   * **Cash** – record income when received, expenses when paid. Use this if you have no inventory.  
   * **Accrual** – record income when earned, expenses when incurred. Required if you keep inventory or if you are a “small business taxpayer” with annual receipts >$31 million. [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)[[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  
   * **Special or combination methods** are allowed if they clearly show income. [[7]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=5)  
   To change your method later you’ll normally need IRS approval via Form 1128 (and possibly a user fee). [[6]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/317-irs_publication_334_tax_guide_small_business.pdf#page=14)  

3. **Record transactions daily**:
   * Keep a **business checkbook** or a digital equivalent. Record each transaction with source, amount, and purpose.  
   * Deposit all daily receipts into the business account.  
   * Make payments by check where possible; for cash payments, keep the receipt and explain the payment in your books. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)  

4. **Reconcile monthly**:
   * Compare your bank statement, checkbook, and books.  
   * Verify that bank charges are entered, that deposits after the statement appear, and that cleared checks are matched.  
   * Correct errors by cross‑checking totals of check stubs, check disbursement journals, deposit amounts, and cash receipt books. [[5]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=14)  

5. **Maintain supporting documents** (receipts, invoices, canceled checks, deposit slips, electronic statements). Your records must support every entry in your books and every line on your tax return. Organize them by year and type of income/expense. [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)[[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

6. **Keep a steady record‑keeping system**:
   * Use journal books (or a digital accounting system) to log each transaction.  
   * Use ledgers to total each account (cash, accounts receivable, inventory, etc.).  
   * Set up a **petty‑cash fund** for small payments; write a petty‑cash slip for each use. [[10]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=13)  

7. **Electronic storage** – if you switch from paper to electronic records, keep the system in a legible format and test it so the IRS can retrieve the same information if needed. [[8]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=12)  

8. **Benifits** – With a clear accounting system you can produce accurate **income statements** (profit‑and‑loss) and **balance sheets**, monitor progress, and prepare tax returns. [[9]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/318-irs_publication_583_starting_a_business.pdf#page=11)  

**Summary**

Write the business plan by following the outline above, finish the executive summary last, and include detailed financial projections and exhibits. For accounting, open a separate business bank account, choose a cash or accrual method (based on inventory and size), record all transactions daily, reconcile every month, keep all supporting documents in a organized system, and use either physical journals and ledgers or a compliant electronic system. These steps ground both your business plan and your ongoing accounting in the guidance found in the supplied segments.

results.question: do i need an ein and what accounting method comes with it
results.answer:
**Do I need an EIN?**  
* If your business will **hire employees** or will have to **pay Federal Excise Tax** you must obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS.  
* A **sole proprietor without employees** may also choose to obtain an EIN to use as a business ID number instead of their Social Security number, but it is not required if you do not hire staff or pay excise.  
[[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=6)

**What accounting method “comes with” an EIN?**  
An EIN does not dictate which accounting method you must use.  When you file your first income‐tax return that includes a Schedule C (Form 1040), you choose an accounting method—either **cash** or **accrual**—based on your business’s inventory needs and other factors.  The choice is independent of whether you have an EIN.

results.question: what forms do i keep for injuries and how long do i keep them

You must keep the OSHA injury and illness record‑keeping forms:

* **OSHA Form 300** – the log of work‑related injuries and illnesses  
* **OSHA Form 301** – the incident report that provides details for each recordable case

results.answer:
To register a trademark:

1. Pick a distinct name or design for your goods or services and check that it isn’t already taken.  
   • Search the trademark databases (both state‑level and federal) to confirm the name is available.  
   — [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)

2. Choose where you want to register.  
   • State‑level registration is done through your state’s Secretary of State office.  
   • Federal registration is handled by the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO).  
   — [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)

3. File the application.  
   • For a state mark, submit a trademark application to the Secretary of State (most states accept online filings).  
   • For a federal mark, file a USPTO application, which can be completed online on the USPTO website.  
   — [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)

4. Pay the required fees.  
   * Fee amounts differ by state and by the type of application (simple, design, etc.).  
   * USPTO fees vary by filing basis (TEAS‑A, TEAS‑B, etc.).  
   — [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)

5. Monitor the application.  
   * If filing at the federal level, the USPTO will examine your file and notify you of any objections or registration.  
   * State offices will likewise review and approve or reject your mark.  
   — [[1]](https://storage.googleapis.com/docsynth-fbb02.appspot.com/workspaces/4219/320-sba_business_planning_guide.pdf#page=10)
